newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bonds, dollar seen taking Fed hike in stride.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bonds, dollar seen taking Fed hike in stride.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond and the dollar are likely to take in stride a much-expected interest rate hike on Tuesday, according to market analysts.
In the latest Reuters poll, 29 out of 37 U.S. primary dealers expected the Federal Open Market Committee to raise the 5.25-percent Fed funds rate by 25 basis points.
"The yield curve will flatten and the bond yield will hold around 7.0 percent," predicted J.P. Morgan senior economist March Wanshel.

Wanshel, one of the few Wall Street economists who, early this year, forecast a spring U.S. rate hike, said the bond yield should not move out of the range established since last year, roughly between 6-3/8 percent and 7-1/4 percent.
"We may eventually get there, but not straight away," Wanshel said of the top of that bond yield range.

"A 25-basis-point hike has been priced into the long end of the market," Wanshel noted. "You have to consider where foreign long-term rates are. In order to bring the U.S. long bond yield above 7.25 percent, you'll need to have a very dramatic correction in the rest of the world."
The 10-year yields of the main government debt issuers are lower than in the United States, meaning investors will continue to be lured by higher returns in the Treasury market.
The 10-year note yields 5.89 percent in Germany, 5.57 percent in Britain, 2.56 percent in Japan and 5.80 percent in France versus 6.73 percent in the United States.

"As long as U.S. inflation appears to be contained and foreign interest rates are where they are, it's difficult to see bond yields go much higher," Wanshel added. "You'll need to have either higher inflation, or much higher foreign yields, or the Fed hiking U.S. rates much higher."

Wanshel, who did not expect the Fed to bring the funds rate higher than 6.0 percent by yearend, said "it would take a lower unemployment rate and signs of upstream inflation, or higher foreign rates, or further rounds of tightening, or any combination of the three to send the bond yield above 7.25 percent."

Kevin Harris, international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch, predicted "the dollar will go up, not very much, not very fast, but it will go up because, at least in the near term, the rate differential will be in favor of the United States."
Harris, paraphrasing Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, noted "1997 is not 1994," meaning there is limited scope for profit-taking on a long bond yielding nearly 7.0 percent.

At the beginning of the last tightening cycle of 1994-early 1995, profit-taking crushed the Treasury market when the long bond yielded a low 6.0 percent and the capital flows out of U.S. assets sent the dollar tumbling.
"Dollar/yen will go back to its recent highs. Dollar/mark will rally at first and stay there unless people start getting worried about hikes totalling 100 basis points or more," Harris added.
The MCM CurrencyWatch international economist said there was no ground at this stage to expect U.S. hikes of such magnitude.

"In the second half, the Fed will make a fresh evalutation of the situation. Right now, they are correcting what they see as a fairly healthy state of growth," Harris added. "The odds are that they won't need to kill growth in the process (of preempting inflation)."
David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston, expected a Fed hike to be constructive for the dollar and flatten the yield curve.

"My guess is that, since we already had a steepening of the yield curve, the hike will have no major impact on long-term rates," Jones noted. "We'll stay in the vicinity of 7.0 percent because the hike has already been largely discounted."
Jones said the expected rate hike will have a positive impact for U.S. assets and the dollar because it will reassure financial markets about the Fed's anti-inflation vigilance.

"Consumer demand has been quite strong and has been applying additional pressure on resources. The economy has been growing faster than its long-term trend potential," Jones pointed out. "The absence of a Fed move in itself would have raised concern over where the Fed sees potential non-inflationary growth."
